title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
Can physics-informed neural networks compete with a classical numerical solver for option pricing? In this project, I implemented and compared three approaches to pricing European call options: Crank–Nicolson, a physics-informed neural network (PINN), and a physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold network (PIKAN).
For the one-dimensional Black–Scholes problem tested, Crank–Nicolson achieved the lowest pricing errors and shortest runtime. PIKAN improved substantially on the baseline PINN’s accuracy, but required considerably more training time.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
Can physics-informed neural networks compete with a classical numerical solver for option pricing? In this project, I implemented and compared three approaches to pricing European call options: Crank–Nicolson, a physics-informed neural network (PINN), and a physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold network (PIKAN).
For the one-dimensional Black–Scholes problem tested, Crank–Nicolson achieved the lowest pricing errors and shortest runtime. PIKAN improved substantially on the baseline PINN’s accuracy, but required considerably more training time.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
Why this problem?
Black–Scholes provides a useful controlled benchmark because European call prices have an analytical solution. This makes it possible to measure approximation errors directly rather than compare numerical methods against another approximate reference.
The aim was to investigate the accuracy and computational cost of physics-informed learning in a setting where a strong classical method already exists.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
How I compared the methods
Crank–Nicolson approximates the pricing equation on a grid, solving a tridiagonal linear system at each time step. The PINN instead represents the price function with a multilayer perceptron, trained to satisfy the differential equation and its initial and boundary conditions. The PIKAN uses the same physics-informed principle with a spline-based Kolmogorov–Arnold network.
For the main experiment, I used a strike price of 100, a one-year maturity, a 5% risk-free rate and 20% volatility. All methods were assessed against analytical prices on the same 100 × 50 evaluation grid.
I evaluated several PINN configurations and two PIKAN training lengths. Performance measures included root mean squared error (RMSE), maximum absolute error, relative L2 error and runtime.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
Main findings
In the main comparison, Crank–Nicolson achieved an RMSE of approximately 0.0098 in 0.29 seconds. The baseline PINN achieved approximately 0.501 in 33.7 seconds, while the PIKAN trained for 3,000 epochs achieved approximately 0.0581 in 257.6 seconds.
The PIKAN therefore offered a clear accuracy improvement over the baseline PINN, although Crank–Nicolson remained both faster and more accurate. Increasing PINN width or adding a learning-rate scheduler did not consistently improve performance, illustrating the importance of testing implementation choices.

Sensitivity to volatility
In a separate sensitivity experiment, I tested volatility values from 10% to 40%. Crank–Nicolson retained the lowest RMSE at every tested value, and PIKAN consistently improved on the baseline PINN.



Pricing RMSE across four volatility assumptions in the sensitivity experiment. Crank–Nicolson achieved the lowest error at each tested value.


Errors increased noticeably for both Crank–Nicolson and PIKAN at 40% volatility. This motivates further investigation of resolution, boundary effects and training choices.
The runtime comparison shows that PIKAN’s improvement over the baseline PINN came at substantial computational cost. Crank–Nicolson runtimes were positive but too small to distinguish clearly on the plotted scale.



Recorded runtime across four volatility assumptions. Neural-network training was substantially more expensive than the Crank–Nicolson solve.

title: Neural Networks vs Classical Option Pricing
text:
What I learned and limitations
The main lesson was the value of a strong numerical baseline. Learning the overall shape of a price surface is not sufficient: accuracy and computational cost must also justify the approach.
These results concern the implementations and problem tested. The neural models differed in parameter counts, training points and training lengths, so the comparison does not isolate architecture alone. Experiments used a laptop without a dedicated CUDA-enabled GPU, and fixed seeds rather than repeated trials across multiple seeds. Reported runtimes concern solving or training, rather than a separate inference-speed benchmark.
The study excludes stochastic volatility, dividends and early exercise. A natural extension is to investigate how the accuracy–cost trade-off changes as problem dimensionality increases, using matched computational budgets and repeated runs.

title: Position Sizing and Risk Management for Systematic Trading
text:
How to use this notebook
Run the cells from top to bottom.
Requirements: Python, NumPy, pandas and Matplotlib.
The example uses one synthetic asset and a constant long signal. This isolates the effect of position sizing from signal generation.
All three methods use the same prices, execution timing and cost model. The 2% target refers to annual standalone volatility relative to portfolio equity. It is not a maximum loss.
The illustrative limits and parameters are purely hypothetical examples.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter

# Model settings
TRADING_DAYS = 252
LOOKBACK = 60
INITIAL_EQUITY = 100_000
RISK_TARGET = 0.02
FIXED_WEIGHT = 0.10
POSITION_CAP = 0.20
COST_RATE = 0.001  # Illustrative one-way cost: 10 basis points

# Save exported charts here
OUTPUT_DIR = Path("outputs")
OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# Match the presentation
BG = "#0E1525"
WHITE = "#F5F7FA"
GREY = "#B4BDCB"
BLUE = "#4EA5F5"
GREEN = "#36C99B"
RED = "#F16B75"

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": BG,
    "axes.facecolor": BG,
    "axes.edgecolor": GREY,
    "axes.labelcolor": WHITE,
    "text.color": WHITE,
    "xtick.color": GREY,
    "ytick.color": GREY,
    "grid.color": "#344256",
    "font.size": 12,
    "savefig.facecolor": BG,
})

print("Setup complete.")

Setup complete.

title: Position Sizing and Risk Management for Systematic Trading
text:
1. Synthetic market data
We simulate three consecutive volatility regimes: - Low volatility: 5% annualised. - Moderate volatility: 20% annualised. - High volatility: 40% annualised.
These are simulation inputs, not values supplied to the sizing rule. The strategy must estimate volatility from observed past returns.
We hold the signal constant at +1 (long) to isolate the effect of sizing.

# Fix the seed so the example reproduces the same simulated path.
# The seed is not selected to optimise strategy performance.

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

days_per_regime = 252

# Simulation inputs change in three regimes.
# The sizing rule cannot observe these inputs; it uses rolling estimates.
annual_vol = np.repeat(
    [0.05, 0.20, 0.40],
    days_per_regime
)

n_days = len(annual_vol)

# Include an initial price before the first simulated return
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=n_days + 1)

# Zero expected daily return: no predictive edge is assumed
simulated_returns = rng.normal(
    loc=0.0,
    scale=annual_vol / np.sqrt(TRADING_DAYS)
)

prices = pd.Series(
    np.r_[50.0, 50.0 * np.cumprod(1 + simulated_returns)],
    index=dates,
    name="price"
)

data = prices.to_frame()
data["return"] = data["price"].pct_change()
data["input_annual_vol"] = np.r_[np.nan, annual_vol]

# Keep direction constant to isolate sizing behaviour.
# No predictive trading edge is assumed.
data["signal"] = 1.0

# Estimate volatility from the latest 60 observed daily returns.
# Annualise using the same 252-day convention as the risk target.
data["estimated_annual_vol"] = (
    data["return"]
    .rolling(LOOKBACK, min_periods=LOOKBACK)
    .std(ddof=1)
    * np.sqrt(TRADING_DAYS)
)

data.tail()

Interpretation
The rolling estimate responds gradually to regime changes because its window contains both older and newer observations.
The dashed line is known only because we generated the data. In a real market, the underlying volatility is not directly observable.
A shorter lookback responds faster but produces a noisier estimate. A longer lookback is smoother but reacts more slowly.

title: Position Sizing and Risk Management for Systematic Trading
section: 2. From volatility estimates to target weights
text:
2. From volatility estimates to target weights
We compare: - A fixed 10% allocation. - A 2% annual standalone risk target divided by estimated volatility. - The same volatility sizing, capped at 20%.
All methods stay in cash until the 60-return estimation window is available. These are target weights calculated at each observation, before execution.

# Only size positions when the volatility estimate is valid.
# Require a complete lookback window and a positive volatility estimate.
# All methods remain in cash until this condition is met.
valid_vol = (
    data["estimated_annual_vol"].notna()
    & (data["estimated_annual_vol"] > 0)
)

target_weights = pd.DataFrame(index=data.index)

target_weights["Fixed allocation"] = (
    FIXED_WEIGHT * data["signal"]
).where(valid_vol, 0.0)

target_weights["Volatility sizing"] = (
    data["signal"]
    * RISK_TARGET
    / data["estimated_annual_vol"].where(valid_vol)
).fillna(0.0)

# Limit the magnitude of the target weight to 20%.
# When this binds, the original standalone volatility target is not met.
target_weights["Volatility sizing + cap"] = (
    target_weights["Volatility sizing"]
    .clip(lower=-POSITION_CAP, upper=POSITION_CAP)
)

target_weights.tail().round(4)

title: Position Sizing and Risk Management for Systematic Trading
text:
3. Execution, costs and portfolio performance
Timing: - Calculate each target using information available after the close. - Execute it at the following day’s close. - The new holding earns returns after execution.
Assumptions: - Fractional shares and full fills are permitted. - Execution costs equal 0.1% of absolute traded value. - Cash earns no interest. - Financing costs, market impact and taxes are excluded. - Targets are sized using equity immediately before execution costs. - Positions remain open at the end; no final liquidation cost is charged.

Timing example

After Monday’s close: calculate a target using information through Monday.
At Tuesday’s close: execute that target.
From Tuesday’s close to Wednesday’s close: the new holding earns its first price return.

Tuesday’s closing price is used as the assumed execution price. Full execution at that price is a modelling assumption.

def run_backtest(prices, targets):
    cash = float(INITIAL_EQUITY)
    shares = 0.0
    previous_equity = float(INITIAL_EQUITY)
    records = []

    # Execute yesterday's target at today's close.
    # Existing shares earn the price move into today's close;
    # newly purchased shares earn price changes only after execution.
    execution_targets = targets.shift(1).fillna(0.0)

    for date, price in prices.items():
        # Mark existing holdings to today's closing price
        equity_before_cost = cash + shares * price

        # Calculate the desired shares using pre-cost equity
        weight = execution_targets.loc[date]
        # Size using equity before costs. Costs slightly change the resulting post-trade weight, so the cap is a target-weight cap in this example.
        desired_shares = weight * equity_before_cost / price

        # Trade the difference from actual holdings, including price-driven drift.
        # A constant target weight can therefore still require rebalancing.
        trade_shares = desired_shares - shares
        trade_value = trade_shares * price
        cost = abs(trade_value) * COST_RATE

        # Execute the trade and pay its cost
        cash -= trade_value + cost
        shares = desired_shares

        equity = cash + shares * price

        records.append({
            "date": date,
            "equity": equity,
            "net_return": equity / previous_equity - 1,
            "turnover": abs(trade_value) / equity_before_cost,
            "cost": cost,
            "shares": shares,
            "actual_weight": shares * price / equity,
        })

        previous_equity = equity

    result = pd.DataFrame(records).set_index("date")

    # Positive drawdown convention, matching the slides
    result["drawdown"] = (
        1 - result["equity"] / result["equity"].cummax()
    )

    return result


backtests = {
    method: run_backtest(data["price"], target_weights[method])
    for method in target_weights.columns
}

print("All three backtests completed.")

All three backtests completed.

title: Position Sizing and Risk Management for Systematic Trading
text:
4. Performance metrics

Total net return: change in equity over the simulation, after execution costs.
Annualised volatility: sample standard deviation of daily net returns multiplied by the square root of 252.
Maximum drawdown: largest percentage decline from a previous equity peak. Drawdown is reported as a positive loss percentage.
Annualised turnover: average daily absolute traded value divided by pre-trade equity, multiplied by 252. Purchases and sales both count.
Total costs: sum of modelled execution costs in euros.

Volatility and turnover use the common evaluation period beginning on the first execution date. Initial entry costs are included. No final liquidation is performed.

first_target_date = data.index[valid_vol][0]
first_target_position = data.index.get_loc(first_target_date)
evaluation_start = data.index[first_target_position + 1]

summary_rows = []

for method, result in backtests.items():
    evaluated = result.loc[evaluation_start:]

    summary_rows.append({
        "Method": method,
        "Total net return": (
            result["equity"].iloc[-1] / INITIAL_EQUITY - 1
        ),
        "Annualised volatility": (
            evaluated["net_return"].std(ddof=1)
            * np.sqrt(TRADING_DAYS)
        ),
        "Maximum drawdown": result["drawdown"].max(),
        "Annualised turnover": (
            evaluated["turnover"].mean() * TRADING_DAYS
        ),
        "Total costs (€)": result["cost"].sum(),
    })

summary = pd.DataFrame(summary_rows).set_index("Method")

display_summary = summary.copy()

percentage_columns = [
    "Total net return",
    "Annualised volatility",
    "Maximum drawdown",
    "Annualised turnover",
]

for column in percentage_columns:
    display_summary[column] = summary[column].map(
        lambda value: f"{value:.2%}"
    )

display_summary["Total costs (€)"] = (
    summary["Total costs (€)"].map(lambda value: f"€{value:,.2f}")
)

display(display_summary)

summary.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "comparison_metrics.csv")

title: Position Sizing and Risk Management for Systematic Trading
text:
5. Findings and limitations
On this simulated path, volatility sizing reduced realised volatility and maximum drawdown relative to the fixed allocation, but increased turnover.
The position cap reduced low-volatility exposure and turnover relative to unconstrained volatility sizing.
All three methods lost money. Position sizing changes risk exposure; it does not create a predictive edge.
These results come from one synthetic path. They do not establish that one method is consistently superior. Average exposures differ across methods.
The model excludes jumps, changing liquidity, partial fills, financing, taxes and realistic market impact. Cash earns no interest.
The notebook implements single-asset sizing and a position cap. It does not implement the lecture’s sector limits, multi-asset correlation checks, portfolio leverage limits or drawdown-response policies.

section: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for Absolutely Continuous Functions
text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for Absolutely Continuous Functions
My undergraduate dissertation at the University of Galway examined how absolute continuity connects differentiation and integration.
The central question is when a function can be recovered by integrating its derivative. Absolute continuity provides the appropriate framework for this form of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
This expository project developed my experience in rigorous mathematical reasoning and communicating a sustained mathematical argument.
